claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing components are predominantly governed by thermally activated grain-boundary sliding.
Grain-boundary sliding enhances dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery.
Reducing grain size through thermomechanical processing should improve plastic strain capacity and overall toughness.
Controlled severe plastic deformation followed by annealing can produce a fine, stable grain structure with increased grain-boundary area.
Above approximately 600°C, thermally activated deformation mechanisms prevail in the proposed refractory-alloy system.
At high temperatures, grain-boundary sliding becomes activated.
Activated grain-boundary sliding assists dislocation motion and dynamic recovery.
Grain refinement increases the total grain-boundary area available for sliding.
Increasing the grain-boundary area available for sliding eases plastic deformation and improves toughness relative to a coarse-grained microstructure.
At high temperature, engineered fine-grained samples will exhibit greater plastic strain before failure than coarse-grained baseline samples.
At high temperature, engineered fine-grained samples will exhibit greater fracture toughness than coarse-grained baseline samples.
In-situ observations will reveal more grain-boundary-sliding activity in engineered fine-grained samples than in coarse-grained samples.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply to refractory metals and similar high-melting-point alloys used in plasma-facing components under high-temperature conditions.
The hypothesis may not hold when brittle intergranular fracture or radiation-induced embrittlement dominates deformation and failure.
The hypothesis may not apply to ceramics because their deformation behavior differs from that of refractory metals.
The relative contributions of dislocation climb and radiation-induced effects under operational fusion conditions are uncertain.
The optimal grain size and the stability of the engineered interfaces have not been determined.
